conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad we’re getting a chance to talk today. I’m Dr. Reyes, a perinatal mental-health clinician whose whole job is to look after new mothers’ emotional well-being. We’re going to use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days; it helps us spot anything from normal “baby blues” all the way to more serious depression or anxiety that deserves extra support. Everything you say stays completely confidential between you and the clinical team, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no right or wrong answers, only your honest experience. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally; we’ll just chat through them one by one.

Let’s start: Over the last week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you used to, or has that been harder lately?

[sighs softly, eyes on the blanket draped over my lap]

It’s… harder. I used to love putting on a podcast and baking banana bread while the baby napped, but last week when I tried, I just stared at the bowl and felt… flat. Like the spark wasn’t there. I still went through the motions, but it felt like I was watching somebody else do it. Even when my partner tried to get me to watch a show we always laughed at, I’d sit there, half-smiling, but not really feeling it inside.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, eyes still low]

Sometimes I can laugh—like when the baby let out this huge burp right as my mom walked in—but it feels forced. I’ll catch myself chuckling and then think, “Shouldn’t I be happier about that?” Most of the time the humor just slips away before it really lands.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet for a moment, twisting the edge of the blanket]

Not really. My sister keeps texting about meeting for coffee next week, and part of me knows I *should* be excited to get out, but when I picture it I just feel… tired and worried—what if the baby cries the whole time, what if I leak through my shirt, what if I can’t think of anything to say? The happy feeling I used to get when I made plans doesn’t show up anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Voice drops, fingers tightening on the blanket]

All the time. Yesterday he wouldn’t settle for his nap—just kept crying—and I kept thinking, *"What am I doing wrong? Other moms seem to calm their babies so easily."* When he finally fell asleep, instead of feeling relieved I sat there crying, convinced it was my fault he was so fussy. Even little things, like spilling a bit of pumped milk, make me feel like I’ve failed him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings the blanket, eyes darting to the bassinet]

Pretty often. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing, thinking, *"Is he breathing okay? What if he spits up and chokes?"* I check the monitor a dozen times a night even when he’s quiet. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the pediatrician said so—but the worry just barges in and I can’t shake it for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses a hand to chest]

Yes… a couple of times this week. Once, I was just folding his tiny onesies and suddenly my heart started pounding so hard I thought I might pass out. I couldn’t pinpoint why—I wasn’t in danger or anything—but I had to sit on the floor and breathe through my mouth until the shaking stopped. It lasted maybe five minutes, but it left me rattled the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

[nods slowly, shoulders sagging]

Most days, yeah. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles, the laundry pile, the texts I haven’t answered, and it feels like a wave crashing over me. Some mornings I cope okay—like yesterday I managed to prep dinner while he napped—but other times I just freeze, thinking, *"I can’t do all this,"* and then I feel worse for not getting it done.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[lets out a shaky breath]

That’s been happening a lot. After the night feedings, when he finally drifts off, my mind keeps spinning— replaying everything I might’ve done wrong, worrying about tomorrow. I lie there exhausted but wide-awake, sometimes for an hour or two. Even when I do sleep, I wake up at every tiny grunt he makes. I’m just… tired all the time.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, eyes welling]

Yeah… most of the day, every day. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be holding him, watching his tiny face, and instead of feeling that rush of love everyone talks about, I just feel this ache in my chest. Sometimes I cry when I’m nursing—not because of pain, just… sad. And then I feel guilty for being sad when he’s healthy and here.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks, tears slipping]

Almost every day this week. Sometimes it’s just quiet tears while I rock him—like I’m too tired to even make a sound. Other times it’s full-on sobbing in the shower so my partner won’t hear. Yesterday I cried because I couldn’t find the matching sock to his outfit. It’s not about the sock, I know, but everything just spills out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, wiping eyes with sleeve]

No—never that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I could never leave him without a mom. When the dark thoughts come, it’s more like *“I’m failing him”* or *“he deserves better,”* but I haven’t thought of hurting myself. I just keep hoping I’ll start feeling like the mom he needs.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style interview, 2 wks post-delivery

Symptoms / Behaviours endorsed  
– Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, anhedonia  
– Marked guilt / self-blame over routine infant-care events  
– Recurrent unprovoked anxiety, nocturnal hypervigilance, two recent panic-like episodes  
– Overwhelm and functional “freezing” when faced with household/infant tasks  
– Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia after night feeds) linked to ruminative worry  
– Appetite not assessed; no self-harm ideation reported; protective toward infant  

Pattern  
High distress across emotional, cognitive, and somatic domains; no safety concerns to self or infant at present.

Screening significance  
Meets provisional cut-off for possible major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; recommend formal EPDS scoring and immediate referral for perinatal mental health evaluation.

Risk factors noted  
Primiparous, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations, limited perceived support, absence of prior psychiatric history per self-report.

Next step  
Discuss findings with patient; offer referral to perinatal psychiatry / counselling and review supports before leaving clinic.
